related.title: Philippine peso gains anew against US dollar amid global fuel price decline
related.text:
The Philippine peso continued its win-streak against the US dollar for the second straight day on Wednesday, still lifted by the decline in global fuel prices.
The local currency gained 10 centavos to close at P63.675:$1, from P63.775:$1 on Tuesday.
In a commentary, Rizal Commercial Banking Corp. chief economist Michael Ricafort said the peso’s strength came “after the recent net decline in global crude oil prices to near three-month lows that could help ease inflationary pressures and also help fundamentally reduce the country’s import bill.”
Ricafort said the peso also posted a “net appreciation” against the US dollar for “nearly a month already since President Marcos gave signals of reassurance on the peso exchange rate since October 28, 2026.”

article.text:
BOTH the peso and the stock market closed stronger on Wednesday, boosted by the continued decline in global oil prices and bargain hunting in heavyweight stocks.
The local currency closed stronger by 10 centavos to P63.675 from Tuesday’s P63.775. It opened at P63.67 and traded from P63.65 to P63.775. The volume reached $1.054 billion, down from the previous day’s total of $1.217 billion.
A trader said the peso appreciated from the continued decline in global crude prices. However, it warned that the local currency “might weaken ahead of a likely strong US PCE report overnight.”
The trader said exchange rates might move between P63.50 and P63.80.
The Philippine Stock Exchange composite index (PSEi), meanwhile, rebounded on Wednesday, gaining 0.68 percent to close at 5,493.41 as investors hunted for bargains in select heavyweight stocks and positioned ahead of the upcoming MSCI rebalancing.
The broader All Shares index also advanced 0.37 percent.
Japhet Tantiangco, research manager at Philstocks Financial Inc., said bargain hunting in heavyweight stocks, including International Container Terminal Services Inc. (ICTSI) and SM Investments Corp., helped lift the benchmark despite broader market weakness.
The services sector led the gainers, climbing 5.09 percent, while the banking sector posted the steepest decline at 4.72 percent.
ICTSI was the PSEi’s strongest performer, surging 6.85 percent, while China Banking Corp. (Chinabank) was the biggest laggard, plunging 28.70 percent as investors took profits following its sharp rally in the previous session.
Tantiangco said the market’s advance came despite negative market breadth, with losers outnumbering gainers 19 to 11 among index constituents, indicating that buying interest was concentrated in selected heavyweight stocks.
He added that declining global bond yields also provided support to the market.
Luis Limlingan, head of sales at Regina Capital Development Corp., said bargain hunting brought the index closer to the 5,500 level as investors accumulated stocks trading at attractive valuations.
He added that positioning ahead of the MSCI rebalancing, particularly in select stocks that had experienced significant price declines, also supported buying interest.
Continued gains in the Philippine peso against the US dollar further helped investor sentiment, Limlingan said.
Despite the market’s advance, foreign investors remained net sellers, recording net outflows of P138.74 million.
Trading activity reached P6.52 billion in net value turnover, excluding extraordinary block sales, according to Limlingan.
The broader market also remained weak, with 82 declining stocks against 97 advancing issues and 53 unchanged, based on Limlingan’s figures.
Tantiangco cautioned that the negative market breadth and foreign outflows pointed to limited conviction behind Wednesday’s rally, leaving the sustainability of the recovery uncertain.

related.title: NFA’s palay procurement lower than target as of end-October
related.text:
THE National Food Authority (NFA) said that, to date, it has procured 175,000 metric tons (MT), or 3.5 million bags of palay (unmilled rice), only about 22 percent of the agency’s 790,000 procurement target for the year due to low harvests from farmers.
NFA Administrator Larry Lacson attributed the low palay procurement to heavy rains that hit crops at a critical stage and reduced farmers’ harvests, a situation he said was confirmed through the agency’s interviews with farmers.
“The volume of rice we are able to procure has decreased, a fact confirmed through our interviews with farmers, who reported a genuine drop in their harvests,” Lacson said.
For instance, the farmers Lacson spoke with in La Union, who typically harvest 100 bags, said they ended up with only 60 bags while they also said their use of fertilizers also declined.
“Furthermore, they said the crops were struck by heavy rains at a critical stage when they should not have been. These are the factors that contributed to the slight decline in procurement,” Lacson told reporters on the sidelines of the recently held Asia-Pacific Conference on Sustainable Agricultural Mechanization 2026.
Despite this, Lacson said the NFA has become more aggressive in terms of pricing, increasing its palay buying price to up to P30 per kilogram for clean and dry palay, with the lowest at P28 per kilogram.
“So with all this, we are hoping that in this last stretch of harvest, this November and early December, we will be able to catch up,” Lacson said.
Latest data from the Philippine Statistics Authority show that palay output in the third quarter of the year reached 3.08 million metric tons (MT), down 17.77 percent from 3.75 million MT in the same period a year ago. Meanwhile, total palay production from January to September fell 5.61 percent to 12.10 million MT from 12.82 million MT last year.
Meanwhile, Lacson assured that no imported rice will be sold at the P20-per-kilogram price, saying that it will remain strictly supplied with locally produced rice and is safe from supply disruptions despite tighter harvests and looming El Niño risks.
“That will never happen that imported rice will be sold in the P20-per-kilogram rice program (Benteng Bigas Meron Na!)... We still have stocks left,” Lacson said.
Instead, he explained that rice imports will go directly into the broader retail market to boost overall national supply, freeing up domestic harvests to sustain both the local market and the P20-per-kilogram rice program.
To ensure the program’s supply alongside the national buffer stock — particularly as lower production volumes slow down procurement — Lacson outlined a two-pronged strategy backed by existing reserves and alternative local sourcing.
He noted that the NFA currently maintains more than eight days’ worth of rice buffer stock and continues to build its inventory, giving the agency a cushion until harvests recover in the first half of next year. CHYNNA GRACE ONG

article.text:
THE National Food Authority (NFA) said procurement of palay (unmilled rice) has hit 22-25% of its 790,000-metric ton (MT) target for the year, citing a decline in palay yields.
NFA Administrator Larry R. Lacson told reporters that current palay stock is around 175,000 MT or around 3.5 million bags. “If we look at our overall target for the year, we’re at 25% only,” he said.
He said palay yields have weakened due to the reduced application of fertilizer, an offshoot of the disruptions caused by the fighting in the Middle East, while unfavorable weather events like the habagat (southwest monsoon) have also affected planting.
Anecdotal reports of falling yields are signaling faltering output all around. In La Union, some farmers have said that the usual 100 bags of palay they harvest has been reduced to 60, Mr. Lacson said.
According to the Philippine Statistics Authority, palay production dropped 17.8% year on year for the third quarter.
Mr. Lacson said the NFA is working on acquiring more stock as storage space can now accommodate around 600,000 MT.
“We are hoping that during this last stretch of harvest, we can still catch up. There is more storage space, and we can accommodate roughly 600,000 MT in capacity. That’s why I always tell farmers to sell their yields to the NFA,” he said.
PALAY PROCUREMENT The NFA is targeting 380,000 MT of palay purchases to support government programs like the “Benteng Bigas, Meron Na!,” which sells subsidized rice for P20 per kilo, as well as to bolster reserve levels.
Mr. Lacson said the current warehouse inventory is equivalent to around eight days’s demand at 300,000 MT, which is being added to.
The NFA’s buying agents are becoming “more lenient” in procurement operations, accepting grain from farmers even when the lot is “borderline” standard quality he said.
The NFA is also awaiting approval to procure storm-damaged palay via Executive Order or when funding is available. Current funding for procurement is limited to standard-quality palay.
Mr. Lacson said mechanization has made even marginal-quality palay saleable.
“This is one of the benefits of NFA’s push for modernization. We have new dryers and rice mills. When we have storm-damaged or below-quality palay… it can be milled instantly. It no longer needs to be store it,” he said. — Maria Mikaela H. Tormon

MANILA, Philippines — Liquefied petroleum gas prices may continue to drop in December following low demand caused by previously high prices, an industry source said Tuesday, November 24.
In an interview with One News, Republic Gas Corp. President Arnel Ty said that LPG prices may slide by an additional P4 to P6 in the coming weeks as contract prices continue to soften.
Increased demand during the holiday season, Ty added, should not pose any issues as the country’s current inventory is enough to last 35 to 45 days.
Consumer-end fuel prices have declined for three weeks in a row as shipments through alternative routes continue to soften crude prices, with LPG firms implementing P2 rollbacks ahead of monthly adjustments in early November.
The Philippines imports most of its petroleum products from the Middle East, leaving domestic fuel prices vulnerable to volatility during times of conflict.
United States President Donald Trump told the media that the Philippines had agreed to purchase “100%” of its energy and agricultural requirements from the US.
Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said at a press briefing Tuesday that no details regarding the energy arrangement have been finalized yet.

article.text:
The Department of Agriculture (DA) has issued a circular that allows the importation of pork products from areas in the United Kingdom that are free from African swine fever (ASF).Under Department Circular No. 58, the DA's Bureau of Animal Industry (BAI) determined the UK maintains tight measures against ASF in several areas."It was determined that the United Kingdom maintains effective veterinary oversight and has implemented appropriate control and risk-mitigating measures, thereby ensuring a low risk of ASF transmission through the importation of live swine, pork, and pork products from its designated zones," the document read.The circular covers importation of live swine and their products, including pork and genetic materials from the United Kingdom.Last August, the DA lifted the temporary ban on the importation of industrially manufactured, hermetically sealed, and heat-treated canned pork products due to the threat of ASF.The DA said that only pork products that have undergone heat treatment in a hermetically sealed contained, industrially manufactured, and canned with valid registration in the Philippines can be imported. —VAL, GMA News

quickHits.summary: THE liquor industry said higher excise taxes on ready-to-drink (RTD) alcoholic beverages could make legitimate products less competitive,…
reasons: reader relevance 2/3: Proposed excise hikes on RTD alcohol could raise prices

article.text:
THE liquor industry said higher excise taxes on ready-to-drink (RTD) alcoholic beverages could make legitimate products less competitive, pushing consumers toward cheaper illicit alternatives instead of discouraging alcohol consumption.
Olivia Limpe-Aw, president of the Distilled Spirits Association of the Philippines (DSAP), told the House of Representatives Ways and Means Committee on Wednesday that RTDs should not face additional tax burdens, noting that some products have alcohol concentrations comparable to beer.
Distilled spirits can be manufactured at alcohol concentrations of 3%, 5% or 7%, depending on the product, similar to the alcohol content of beer, she said.
She noted that RTDs are already subject to the tax imposed on distilled spirits, including a 22% ad valorem tax based on net retail prices, on top of the applicable specific excise tax.
Ms. Limpe-Aw said RTDs have emerged to cater to younger consumers, and not because manufacturers are seeking to benefit from differences in tax rates.
“If you raise the tax on RTDs, then it’s being unfair also to that market,” she said.
She warned that further increases could discourage consumers from purchasing these products, affecting manufacturers and government revenue.
Minerva Dela Cruz of the Association of Beverage Alcohol Producers of the Philippines (ABAPI) said higher prices for legitimate, tax-paid alcoholic beverages could undermine the government’s efforts to reduce harmful drinking.

Climate change has suffered another setback when the recent Climate Change Summit in Turkey virtually collapsed.
The Climate Change Summit is an international conference organized under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. It brings together around 200 countries to discuss how the world can respond to global warming and its consequences. The conference is commonly called COP which stands for Conference of the Parties. It has several major objectives. First, to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. It encourages countries to reduce carbon dioxide, methane and other gases responsible for global warming. Second, to motivate countries to transition to renewable energy. This means to encourage the use of solar, wind, hydroelectric and other cleaner energy sources instead of depending heavily on fossil fuels like coal, oil and natural gas.
